explanations.answer: Allowed isn't always good for you
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Paul, the apostle writing to the church in Corinth, says “but not everything is beneficial.” Being allowed to do something and it being good for you are two different things. I'm allowed to eat the whole batch of dough before it hits the oven. Doesn't mean my stomach will send me a thank you note.

Close, but Paul doesn't lock the bakery doors. He doesn't take the line back at all. He says “Everything is permissible for me…” and then adds “but not everything is beneficial.” So the question isn't "what am I banned from?" It's "what actually does me good?"

Paul doesn't sort people into the free ones and the not-free ones here. The line he writes is “Everything is permissible for me…” and his "but" is about whether things are beneficial. His point is about what helps, not about who gets a pass. Nobody's standing at a velvet rope checking names.

Yes, he says it right there: “but I will not be mastered by anything.” Think about your phone buzzing and you drop everything to look. That's a little thing running the show. Paul says nothing gets to be his boss, and I say amen to that.

It's actually true. The second time he writes the line, Paul finishes it with “but I will not be mastered by anything.” He's saying nothing gets to boss him around. That's different from the first "but," which was about what's beneficial.

Paul says the opposite. Right after the line about food and the stomach, he writes, “but God will destroy them both.” Food and the stomach have an end date. My best batch of cookies doesn't even last until dinner, so I get it.

That's right, friend. Paul writes, “but God will destroy them both.” Food and the stomach aren't forever things. I've watched a whole tray of cookies disappear in ten minutes, and nobody was surprised.

You've got it. Paul says the body is “…for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.” It goes both directions. The body isn't a spare part sitting in a drawer, and I would know, since I spent years in a junk drawer myself. It belongs in the Lord's hands, and I can tell you hands are a good place to be.

Paul goes somewhere else with it. He says the body is “…for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.” Later in this same passage he says, “You are not your own…” So "mine alone" isn't where he lands, friend.

Not quite. The world doesn't get named at all in that line. Paul says the body is “…for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.” The Lord is the one he points to, not the crowd, the culture, or the neighbors.

Yes, friend. Paul writes, “By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also.” The same power that did it for the Lord is the power behind the promise for us. That's why Paul can talk about the body as something that matters. It isn't a throwaway.

I love a good name, but that's not what Paul says here. He says God raised the Lord from the dead, and “…He will raise us also.” The promise is resurrection. A new name tag isn't mentioned anywhere in the verse.

Look at the order Paul uses. God raised the Lord from the dead, and “…He will raise us also.” Raising someone from the dead is a different promise than keeping someone from dying. The verse names the raising.

Paul says the opposite, and he doesn't whisper it. He asks, “Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute?” and answers with one word: “Never!” He's reminding them that their bodies are members of Christ. This part of the letter is heavy, so I'll keep it plain: he says no.

That's right, friend. Paul asks, “Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute?” and then answers, “Never!” He starts from the fact that their bodies are members of Christ. This is a heavy part of the letter, and he doesn't water it down.

explanations.answer: He is one with her in body
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. Paul says, “…he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body?” Then he backs it up with Scripture: “The two will become one flesh.” He's showing that the joining is real, and he says so plainly.

Paul says the opposite. He writes that such a man “…is one with her in body?” Paul backs that up with the Scripture he quotes about two becoming one flesh. He describes the man as one with her, right in the middle of it.

explanations.answer: Only she is affected by it
explanations.explanation: Paul puts the man right in the middle of it. He says “…he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body?” That joining involves both people, and Paul says it about the man in the verse. So he doesn't treat it as something that only touches her.

Yes, friend. Paul writes, “But he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit.” After all that talk about being joined in body, he turns it around. Being one with the Lord goes deep, and I'm glad he said so.
Nobody's pulling out a ladder here. Paul writes that the one who unites himself with the Lord “…is one with Him in spirit.” It's not about who's higher or lower. It's about being joined to Him.
Wealth doesn't come up in that verse. Paul says the one who unites himself with the Lord “…is one with Him in spirit.” The verse is about being joined to Him.

explanations.answer: It is a sin against his own body
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Paul says, “Every other sin a man can commit is outside his body, but he who sins sexually sins against his own body.” That's why he gives the short command first: “Flee from sexual immorality.” Paul puts that command right at the front.

explanations.answer: It only harms the other person
explanations.explanation: Paul points back at the man himself. He says that “…he who sins sexually sins against his own body.” So it isn't only about the other person. He's saying this one touches the sinner's own body in a way the other sins don't.

explanations.answer: It is a sin nobody can see
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't talk about who can see it. His point is where the sin lands: “…he who sins sexually sins against his own body.” That's what he sets against every other sin, which he says is outside the body. He keeps the focus on the body.

explanations.answer: A temple of the Holy Spirit
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Paul writes, “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you…?” The Holy Spirit lives in them. That makes the body a special place, not just the thing that gets you to work on time.

Paul never talks about the body like a jail cell. He says, “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you…?” A temple is a place where someone dwells. He's saying the Holy Spirit is in them.
A tool sits in a toolbox. Paul says something bigger: “…your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you…” That's a place for the Holy Spirit, not just equipment.

Yes, friend. Paul writes about “…the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God?” They received Him from God. It's right there in the same verse as the temple. That's a lot of truth packed into one verse.
It's actually true. Paul says the Holy Spirit is the one “…who is in you, whom you have received from God?” So the Holy Spirit came to them from God. It's right there in the same verse as the temple.

That's the word, friend. After saying “You are not your own; you were bought at a price,” Paul says, “Therefore glorify God with your body.” That "Therefore" ties it all together. The body is for the Lord, so Paul tells them to use it to glorify Him.

Paul says the opposite right before his command. He writes, “You are not your own; you were bought at a price.” Then comes the "Therefore" and he tells them to “…glorify God with your body.” So keeping it for themselves isn't what he tells them.

Paul doesn't tell anyone to tune out their body. Earlier he says it's a temple of the Holy Spirit, and that God “…will raise us also.” Then he says, “Therefore glorify God with your body.” The body matters now, not just later.
